items.title: L14: Why build an evidence portfolio
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: A promotion application is rarely a single answer. It is a set of pieces of evidence, which may include written statements for lead Behaviours, a CV, a personal statement, test results and the interview, and the whole is assessed as an impression of whether you can do the role. A portfolio approach means planning the whole set of evidence before writing any of it. Start with a grid. In one axis list every element the advert assesses: each Behaviour, any Strengths, Ability, Technical requirements and Experience. On the other axis list your candidate examples, perhaps six to ten significant pieces of work from the last two or three years. Mark which example could best evidence which element, and look for three things: gaps, where nothing supports an element; clusters, where one example is carrying too much; and mismatches, where the example is real but pitched below the target grade. The aim is not to use every example but to give each element its strongest honest support, with as little repetition as possible. A good portfolio usually shows range: different kinds of work, different groups of people, different scales, and a mix of what went well and what was learned. It also shows coherence: the examples add up to a recognisable professional who is ready for the next grade. Do not choose examples only because they are impressive; choose them because they fit the element and you can talk about them in depth. Finally, remember that evidence is cumulative: a thin example for one Behaviour can be offset by stronger evidence elsewhere only if the advert allows, and in many processes each Behaviour must pass separately. Check the scoring rules.

questions.prompt: What does a portfolio approach to a promotion application involve?

options.text: Writing the strongest statement first and fitting the rest around it
Choosing examples only after each question has been seen at interview
Planning the whole set of evidence before writing any of it
Copying the structure of a successful colleague's application

questions.prompt: In the grid method, what goes on the two axes?

options.text: The Behaviours in the advert and the grades of your managers
The elements the advert assesses and your candidate examples
Your past roles and the dates you held each of them
The stages of the process and the panel members at each

questions.prompt: Which problem is shown when one example appears to support five Behaviours?

options.text: A cluster, where one example is carrying too much
A gap, where one Behaviour has no example to support it
A mismatch, where the example is pitched below the grade
A strength, because one example can cover many elements

questions.prompt: What does a mismatch in the grid describe?

options.text: A real example that is pitched below the target grade
An example that appears twice in the same statement
An example for which the candidate has no dates or figures
An example that was led by a colleague rather than the candidate

questions.prompt: What is the aim in allocating examples to elements?

options.text: Every example is used at least once across the application
Each element gets its strongest honest support with little repetition
The most impressive example supports the lead Behaviour and as many others as it can
Each element is supported by whichever example is most recent

questions.prompt: Which feature suggests a well-balanced portfolio?

options.text: A single large project described from several angles
Range in kinds of work, people, scale and in successes and lessons
Examples drawn only from the current role and the current team
Examples that all show the same Behaviour at the highest level

questions.prompt: Why is choosing examples only because they are impressive a risk?

options.text: Assessors always mark down any example that involves a large budget
The word limit makes it impossible to describe an impressive example
They may not fit the element and may be hard to discuss in depth
Impressive examples are normally kept for the interview only

questions.prompt: In many processes, how might Behaviours be scored?

options.text: All are added together, so one weak example is always cancelled out
Only the lead Behaviour is scored once the sift has been passed
Each may need to be passed separately, so a thin one cannot always be offset
Scores are averaged and the result is checked against the grade only

questions.prompt: Why start planning early?

options.text: Applications submitted early are read first and score more highly
The best examples may need to be dug out of old records and checked
Closing dates are normally extended if the advert is not clear
The panel prefers candidates who have prepared earlier than others

questions.prompt: Which source helps recall dates and facts for an example?

options.text: The advert and the job description of the new post
A friend outside work who remembers what you said at the time
Your general memory of how the work went overall
Emails, performance reviews and a colleague who can confirm details

items.title: L14: Spreading evidence across the Behaviours
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Promotion adverts often ask for statements on only one or two lead Behaviours, but interviews can cover others, and some processes ask for a statement for every Behaviour. In either case, the way examples are spread matters. Consider a candidate with five significant pieces of work: a restructure of a team, a complaints project, a rotation to another department, a supplier dispute and a response to an audit. A poor spread would use the restructure for Leadership, Developing Others, Changing and Improving and Working Together, leaving the other work unused and making the application look narrow. A better spread might use the restructure for Leadership, the complaints project for Changing and Improving and Managing a Quality Service, the supplier dispute for Communicating and Influencing, the rotation for Working Together and Seeing the Big Picture, and the audit response for Making Effective Decisions. Where one example is the strongest for two Behaviours, consider whether the actions you describe are really different. If you must reuse, use distinct actions and results for each, and keep the setting description brief. A single large project can legitimately support several Behaviours, but a panel may feel that an application relying on it is thin, and may probe heavily to test depth. If an example cannot be spared, it may be better to find a weaker but separate example for the second Behaviour, provided it is at the right level. Be sure not to inflate the second example to compete with the first. When in doubt, favour fit, honesty and depth over breadth for its own sake. Remember too that a non-lead Behaviour may need only a short example for the interview, so a smaller piece of work may suffice.

questions.prompt: In the five-project example, which spread is stronger?

options.text: Giving each project to the Behaviour it fits best, the restructure to Leadership
Using the restructure for four Behaviours and the other projects once each
Using the biggest project for every Behaviour to keep the story simple
Using only the audit response because it shows the widest scope

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of using one large project for four Behaviours?

options.text: The project will be treated as too small to show several Behaviours
The statement will exceed the word count as the context repeats
Panels dislike restructures because they involve many people
The application looks narrow and the panel may probe the depth of the project

questions.prompt: If an example is the strongest fit for two Behaviours, what should the candidate check?

options.text: Whether the example is the more recent of the two candidates
Whether the actions described for each Behaviour are really different
Whether the manager would prefer one Behaviour to be used
Whether the example can be described in fewer than 100 words

questions.prompt: When reusing an example, what should be brief?

options.text: The account of the candidate's actions
The statement of the result achieved
The description of the setting
The link to the wording of the Behaviour

questions.prompt: Why might a weaker separate example be better than reusing a strong one?

options.text: It broadens the application, provided it is at the right level and honest
Weaker examples are scored more generously because they seem modest
Panels penalise any use of the same example twice in the application
It shows that the candidate has kept the strongest example in reserve

questions.prompt: What must not happen when selecting a second example?

options.text: It must not come from the same financial year as the first
It must not be inflated to compete with the first
It must not involve any colleague who was named in the first
It must not be shorter than the first in the statement

questions.prompt: A non-lead Behaviour may be tested at interview. What is often enough?

options.text: A full written statement of the same length as the lead Behaviour
A general account of your approach with no particular example
A short example drawn from a smaller piece of work
The same example as the lead Behaviour, with extra context added

questions.prompt: Which phrase describes the right priority when in doubt?

options.text: Breadth of examples over honesty about the candidate's role
Impressiveness of scale over fit with the Behaviour wording
Fit, honesty and depth over breadth for its own sake
Length of description over the depth of the candidate's own part

questions.prompt: A candidate lists five projects but all demonstrate the same skill. What does this suggest?

options.text: A strong portfolio, because several examples are always better than one
A balanced range, because every example has the same result
An overuse of leadership verbs, which should be replaced by other words
A narrow range even though there are several examples

questions.prompt: Which allocation is the most sensible for a rotation to another department?

options.text: Delivering at Pace only, since a rotation is a short fixed-term move
Working Together and Seeing the Big Picture, where the actions fit
Developing Self and Others only, since a rotation is a learning step
Any Behaviour that has no example yet, whatever the actions were

items.title: L14: One large project across several Behaviours
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Senior candidates often have one major piece of work that dominates their record, such as a transformation programme or a response to a crisis. It is tempting to build every answer from it. Doing so can be acceptable, but it takes care. Each Behaviour has its own verbs and its own test, so the key is to choose a different strand of the project for each. For example, suppose the candidate led a service redesign. For Changing and Improving, the strand might be the case for change, the design choices and the benefits measured. For Making Effective Decisions, it might be a single hard choice: whether to pause the rollout after a pilot showed unexpected errors. For Leadership, it might be a period when morale fell and the candidate held the team together. For Working Together, it might be negotiating roles with a supplier. For Communicating and Influencing, it might be winning over a sceptical board. Describe only the relevant strand and give the project one or two lines of context. Keep the results specific to each strand. The assessors will recognise the project, so brevity in context helps. Avoid repeating the same facts, such as the same savings figure, in several answers, since that suggests thin evidence. A candidate should be prepared for an interview panel to ask about the whole project, and for follow-up questions that test whether the personal role was as described. If your part in the project was narrow, using it for many Behaviours may expose that. If you led it, ensure that each strand was your own decision or action rather than your team's. Where you can, add a second, smaller example in a different setting to show a pattern.

questions.prompt: What is the key to using one large project for several Behaviours?

options.text: Repeat the same summary of the project in each answer
Use the whole project for the lead Behaviour and none for the others
Describe the project's results in full in every answer
Choose a different strand of the project for each Behaviour

questions.prompt: For Making Effective Decisions, which strand of a service redesign would fit best?

options.text: Deciding whether to pause the rollout after a pilot showed unexpected errors
Describing the overall benefits that the redesign achieved for users
Explaining the project plan to staff at the start of the programme
Chairing the weekly project board and keeping its record of actions

questions.prompt: For Leadership, which strand of the project is best?

options.text: Reporting the full costs of the programme to the finance team in detail
Listing the suppliers who were used in each stage of the work
Holding the team together when morale fell
Drawing the detailed process maps for the new service design

questions.prompt: How much context should each answer give about the project?

options.text: A full page for each answer, so each stands alone
None at all, because the Behaviour wording is enough
The whole history of the programme from its first proposal
One or two lines, since assessors will recognise it

questions.prompt: What does repeating the same savings figure across several answers suggest?

options.text: That the savings were unusually large and so worth mentioning often
That the candidate has a careful approach to using exact figures
That the figure is reliable because it appears in several places
That the candidate's evidence is thin

questions.prompt: What might follow at interview if the project dominates the application?

options.text: Questions about it are unlikely, since the statement has already been scored
Questions only about other projects the candidate has not mentioned
Questions about the whole project and the candidate's personal role in it
Questions about the grade of everyone who worked on the project

questions.prompt: Why might using a project for many Behaviours expose a narrow role?

options.text: The panel will assume the role was larger than the candidate says
The panel can test whether each strand was truly the candidate's own
The panel will not read strands that sound too similar to each other
The panel will skip the project and ask about something else entirely

questions.prompt: What can help show that a Behaviour is a pattern rather than a one-off?

options.text: Repeating the same example with a different emphasis each time
Quoting the manager's view of how often the candidate did it
Using longer sentences to show the habit in the same example
Adding a second, smaller example in a different setting

questions.prompt: How should results be treated across strands?

options.text: Use one overall result for every strand to keep things consistent
Leave out results from later strands to avoid repeating figures
Use the team's combined results because they are easy to check
Keep them specific to each strand

questions.prompt: Which attribution check matters most when the candidate led the project?

options.text: That the project had a name that the panel would recognise
That each strand was the candidate's own decision or action, not just the team's
That the project was completed within the most recent year
That the project was large enough to involve ministers

items.title: L14: Balancing success and learning in a portfolio
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: An application built only from triumphs can read as unreal, while one that dwells on failure can look unready. A balanced portfolio includes mainly strong, successful examples, with a small number that show learning from something that did not go to plan. Assessors generally value honesty about setbacks when it is accompanied by ownership and change. A learning example needs a structure of its own: what you intended, what went wrong, what you did when you realised, what you changed afterwards and what happened next time. The final element matters most. A story that ends 'I learned a lot' without showing changed practice is weak, whereas one that ends 'and the next time I faced a similar choice, I did X, which resulted in Y' is strong. Choose a setback that was real but not disastrous or dishonest: it should show the Behaviour even in difficulty, such as Making Effective Decisions after a decision that proved partly wrong, or Developing Others after a coaching approach that did not work. Avoid blaming others, and avoid mistakes that suggest poor integrity, such as breaching security or misleading a colleague, unless the story is about how you reported and put it right and the advert invites such an answer. Strengths and weaknesses questions at interview, such as 'Tell us about a time you made a mistake', draw on the same material, so a prepared learning example is useful there. Where a success contains a smaller failure within it, describing it adds credibility. Do not manufacture a setback that did not happen. Equally, do not present a failure as if it were a success; assessors will see through the spin. Treat any mistakes involving other people with discretion, and describe them in general terms.

questions.prompt: What does a balanced portfolio usually contain?

options.text: Only examples of failure, to prove honesty to the panel
Only successes, since setbacks suggest the candidate is not ready
Mainly strong examples with a small number showing learning from setbacks
An equal number of failures and successes in every statement

questions.prompt: Which structure suits a learning example?

options.text: Problem, who was to blame, apology and a return to normal practice
What you intended, what went wrong, your response, what changed and what followed
Success, a minor difficulty, success again and a summary for the panel
Instruction, completion, feedback from a manager and closure of the task

questions.prompt: Which ending makes a learning example strong?

options.text: I learned a great deal from the experience and I am grateful for it
I will approach any similar situation differently in future
The next time I faced a similar choice I did X, which resulted in Y
It taught me a great deal about my own strengths and limits

questions.prompt: Which setback is suited to a Making Effective Decisions example?

options.text: A decision that proved partly wrong, and the candidate's response
A decision taken by a manager that the candidate carried out
A decision with no real consequences for anyone affected
A routine decision made many times before in the same way

questions.prompt: Why avoid blaming others in a learning example?

options.text: Blame is never allowed to appear in any written statement
It makes the example too long to fit within the word limit
It undermines ownership, which assessors look for
It makes the setback look larger than it really was

questions.prompt: What is the right approach to mistakes that suggest poor integrity?

options.text: Include them to show maximum honesty about the candidate's record
Avoid them, unless the focus is reporting and correcting them and the advert invites it
Describe them in full detail so that the panel can judge for itself
Blame the system so that the candidate's integrity is not questioned

questions.prompt: Why might a prepared learning example help at interview?

options.text: Interview questions about mistakes draw on the same material
Interviews never ask about mistakes at senior grades
It reduces the number of questions that the panel may ask
It replaces the need for other examples in the application

questions.prompt: Which approach to choosing a setback would damage credibility most?

options.text: Choosing one that was real but caused little harm
Inventing one that did not happen to look balanced
Describing it in general terms to protect colleagues
Showing the change in practice that followed it

questions.prompt: What is the effect of presenting a failure as if it were a success?

options.text: It will raise the score because outcomes are all that matter
It will shorten the answer and so leave room for other points
It will be ignored because assessors score only the stated result
Assessors will see through the spin and doubt the candidate's honesty

questions.prompt: How should mistakes involving other people be described?

options.text: In full detail, with names, so that the account can be verified
With discretion and in general terms
By placing the responsibility on the other person involved
By leaving out the other person's role while keeping the result

items.title: L14: Building coherence across stages
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: A senior promotion process may include several stages, such as an application form, an ability test, a written statement and an interview. A candidate who treats each as a separate exercise can contradict themselves; one who builds the whole as a story of readiness for the next grade usually performs better. Coherence has three parts. The first is consistency of facts: dates, figures, titles and your role in each example must match across the documents, since panels compare them. The second is consistency of identity: the examples should present a recognisable professional, with strengths that the CV, statement and interview answers all support. If your statement presents you as a careful analyst and your interview presents you as a risk-taker, the panel will wonder which is true. The third is consistency of level: examples should be pitched at or near the target grade throughout, rather than the statement being senior and the interview examples junior. Preparation for coherence includes keeping copies of everything you submit, listing the facts you stated, and rehearsing how you will expand on each example in speech. At interview, the panel may refer to your statement, so be ready to say more than is written without contradicting it. Also prepare to link examples: a short sentence such as 'that experience also shaped the way I approached the later project' can show development over time. If you realise that something in your application was inaccurate, correct it at the earliest opportunity, since honesty is a Civil Service value and a correction earns more respect than a discovered error. Finally, check that the story fits the role: the evidence you emphasise should be what the advert most needs, not simply what you most enjoy describing.

questions.prompt: What are the three parts of coherence across stages?

options.text: Consistency of facts, identity and level
Consistency of length, tone and formatting
Consistency of dates, names and places only
Consistency of strengths, ability and experience scores

questions.prompt: Which pairing would make a panel doubt who the candidate really is?

options.text: Both stages describe the same role with the same dates
Both stages use the same figures for the main result
The statement is longer than the interview answer by a wide margin
The statement shows a careful analyst and the interview shows a risk-taker

questions.prompt: Which pairing would make a panel doubt the candidate works at the target grade?

options.text: A senior statement followed by junior interview examples
Two examples chosen at the same grade for the same Behaviour
Both parts using figures to describe the scale of results
A statement and an interview that use the same example

questions.prompt: What should a candidate do if they find an inaccuracy in their application?

options.text: Correct it at the earliest opportunity
Wait to see whether anyone notices before saying anything
Avoid mentioning it, since the error is unlikely to matter
Change the story at interview to fit the correct facts quietly

questions.prompt: Why keep copies of everything submitted?

options.text: To check facts and be consistent when expanding at interview
To send to other departments as evidence of earlier applications
To prove the word count was met if the panel asks
To prepare a different story for each stage of the process

questions.prompt: What can a short linking sentence do?

options.text: Reduce the word count by removing the context of each
Show development over time between examples
Remove the need for results in the second example
Replace the Behaviour wording with the candidate's own

questions.prompt: How should the emphasis of evidence be chosen?

options.text: To match what the candidate most enjoys describing to the panel
To match what the advert most needs
To match the longest example in the candidate's records
To match the example that was completed most recently

questions.prompt: Why might a panel compare documents?

options.text: To check the formatting and layout of each submitted document
To count the number of strong verbs used in each statement
To measure the length of the statement against the limit
To check that facts and roles match across the application

questions.prompt: At interview, what should a candidate be ready to do about the statement?

options.text: Repeat the statement word for word to show consistency
Avoid referring to it, so that the answers stay fresh
Say more than is written without contradicting it
Replace it with a new story that fits the question better

questions.prompt: What does a 'recognisable professional' mean in a portfolio?

options.text: A person who has held one particular job title for a long time
Examples that together present a coherent person ready for the next grade
A person who is strong in a single skill that the role needs
A person whose examples all come from one team and one period

items.title: L14: Lead and non-lead Behaviours: depth and coverage
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: When an advert names lead Behaviours, the candidate has to decide how to divide effort between depth and coverage. Depth means preparing a full, richly detailed example with the actions and result clear, well rehearsed, and able to survive probing. Coverage means having at least a sound example for every Behaviour that could be asked about. The right balance depends on the process. If only the lead Behaviours are assessed at sift and nothing else is formally scored, depth on those matters most. If the interview tests other Behaviours too, a gap in coverage can lose marks that depth elsewhere cannot recover. A practical plan is to prepare lead Behaviour examples to full depth, with a primary and a back-up example in case the panel asks for a second; then prepare a short example for each other Behaviour with the key facts: situation, action, result and the candidate's own decisions, so that it can be delivered in a few minutes. Practise saying each aloud and timing it. Another aspect is the choice of the lead example: the lead Behaviours for senior roles often involve scope across teams and external partners, so the example must be of that scale. Do not spend all your time on the lead and risk being caught out by a question on, say, Developing Self and Others. Equally, do not spread so thinly that no example survives a second question. A final point is that the questions at interview may not mention the Behaviour by name. A question such as 'Tell us about a time you had to change your mind' may touch Making Effective Decisions or Changing and Improving, so be ready to select the example that best fits, even if the wording is loose.

questions.prompt: What does depth mean when preparing a Behaviour example?

options.text: A full, detailed example that can survive probing
A long list of the projects worked on in the last three years
A summary of one project written for a general audience
A reference from a manager confirming that the work was done

questions.prompt: What does coverage mean in preparing Behaviour examples?

options.text: A long statement for the lead Behaviour covering several others
A list of every project the candidate has been involved in
A sound example for every Behaviour that could be asked
A copy of the advert's Behaviour wording with notes against it

questions.prompt: Why might a gap in coverage matter more than extra depth elsewhere?

options.text: Marks lost on a Behaviour with no example cannot be regained elsewhere
Depth is never rewarded in an interview for a senior post
Coverage is the only criterion that panels actually score
The panel marks only the first answer given by a candidate

questions.prompt: What is a practical plan for lead Behaviours?

options.text: Prepare one example in full and a single sentence for any other
Rely on the statement to answer every question the panel asks
Prepare a very short example for each, as the panel will not probe
Prepare a primary and a back-up example in full depth

questions.prompt: What should a short example for a non-lead Behaviour contain?

options.text: The full history of the project and the names of the people involved
A list of all the people involved and their grades
Situation, action, result and the candidate's own decisions
A statement of the candidate's general preference for this work

questions.prompt: Why practise aloud and time each example?

options.text: To increase the number of words available in the answer
To avoid the need to write the example down at all
To make sure it can be delivered clearly in a few minutes
To replace the written statement with a spoken version

questions.prompt: What risk comes from spreading preparation too thinly?

options.text: Examples become too long to deliver in the time allowed
Examples become too similar to each other in the language used
Examples become too recent to be verified by referees
None of the examples survives a second question

questions.prompt: A question 'Tell us about a time you had to change your mind' might touch which Behaviours?

options.text: Making Effective Decisions or Changing and Improving
Delivering at Pace only, since changing your mind causes delay
Working Together only, since it involves agreeing with others
Managing a Quality Service only, since it involves correcting errors

questions.prompt: What should be done when a question does not name a Behaviour?

options.text: Ask the panel to name the Behaviour before answering
Choose the example that best fits what is being asked
Give a general answer about how you usually work
Say the question was covered in the written statement

questions.prompt: Why must a lead example be of a certain scale for a senior role?

options.text: Smaller examples are never accepted in a senior application
The panel dislikes small examples whatever their quality
Lead Behaviours only apply to people who manage a large team
Senior lead Behaviours usually involve scope across teams and partners

items.title: L14: Auditing your own examples
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Before writing, a candidate can audit each example with a short scoring routine. For each example, rate four dimensions out of three. Scope: does it extend beyond your own desk, to a team, a service, several teams or the system? Independence: did you decide the approach, or were you directed? Evidence: can you describe your actions and result with specifics, and could you defend them under questioning? Fit: how clearly does it show the verbs of the Behaviour you intend to use it for? A score of two or three on each suggests a strong example, whereas a one on scope or independence indicates a junior example, and a one on evidence suggests it is too vague or too reliant on the team. The audit also reveals whether the example is worth strengthening: sometimes a low evidence score simply means you need to find the figures or check the dates, whereas a low scope score cannot be fixed by writing. Do the audit honestly; it is no use to score yourself generously. It helps to ask a trusted colleague, who may know what you did, which examples they would pick, though they might see an example differently. If a candidate has several examples with low scope, the answer may be to seek a different role, an acting-up opportunity or a project to widen scope before applying; a promotion application is easier when the evidence already exists. An audit can also show that a longer-standing example is better than a recent one, because of its scope. If so, check whether the advert places any limit on how old evidence can be, and consider briefly explaining why an older example is used. Keep the audit in a simple table and update it as your experience grows.

questions.prompt: Which four dimensions does the audit score?

options.text: Date, length, grade and the manager's opinion
Scope, independence, evidence and fit
Pace, quality, cost and risk attached to the work
Strengths, ability, technical skill and experience of the candidate

questions.prompt: A score of one on independence suggests what?

options.text: The example is junior because the candidate was directed
The example is strong because the candidate followed instructions
The example is too long because it covers other people's work
The example is too recent for the panel to verify properly

questions.prompt: What is the usual remedy for a low evidence score?

options.text: Choose a different Behaviour for the example without checking
Find the figures and check the dates so the example can be defended
Remove the example from the portfolio altogether and start again
Add adjectives that make the example sound more impressive

questions.prompt: Why can a low scope score not be fixed by writing?

options.text: The work itself had limited reach, so wording cannot change it
The scope is set by the advert and not by the candidate's work
Scope is not important to the panel at this grade of post
Scope is a matter of taste and differs between assessors

questions.prompt: Why is honest scoring important?

options.text: The scores are submitted to the panel with the statement
The scoring is a required part of the application form
A generous score gives a false picture of the portfolio
The scores decide the date of the interview

questions.prompt: What may help a candidate whose examples all have low scope?

options.text: Rewriting the examples in more senior language before applying
Using the same examples for several Behaviours to hide the gap
Seeking a role, acting-up or project that widens scope before applying
Applying anyway with a long statement that stresses effort

questions.prompt: Why consider asking a trusted colleague to review?

options.text: They can write the statement on your behalf for submission
They may know what you did and can say which examples they would pick
They can mark the statement the way the panel would mark it
They can submit the application and answer the sift questions

questions.prompt: Why take care with a colleague's view of an example?

options.text: Colleagues are never reliable about what happened in a project
Colleagues must not be shown any part of an application
Colleagues always score examples generously to be kind
They might see the example differently, especially if their role differed

questions.prompt: When might an older example be better than a recent one?

options.text: Never, since only evidence from the last year is accepted
If its scope is greater, provided the advert allows older evidence
Always, since older examples have had time to show results
Only if the older example was more successful than the recent one

questions.prompt: How should the audit be kept?

options.text: In the statement itself so the panel can see the scores
In an email to the recruitment team before the closing date
In the CV, beside each of the roles you have held
In a simple table that can be updated as experience grows

items.title: L14: Evidence from outside the day job at senior grade
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Senior candidates often have strong evidence in activities outside their core duties: chairing a staff network, leading a cross-government working group, acting as a school governor or trustee, coaching or mentoring, leading a volunteering project, or serving on a trade union committee. These can legitimately evidence Behaviours, and may supply scope that a candidate's formal post lacks. For example, running a staff network of several hundred members involves Leadership, Communicating and Influencing, Working Together and Developing Others, and may include budget and accountability. Sitting on a governing body involves Making Effective Decisions and Seeing the Big Picture in a wider setting. Such evidence works best when the candidate shows that the activity was real and substantial: the scale, the responsibility, the decisions taken and the results. It must also be relevant to the grade; a role that involves occasional administrative help is not equivalent to chairing a committee. Check the advert for any restriction, such as whether unpaid experience counts. Be aware of rules: activities that touch on political matters, such as party activity, may conflict with the requirements on civil servants, and trade union duties and equality network roles are normally recognised but should be described in line with departmental policy. Avoid claiming credit for things that others did. Also take care not to use official time or resources inappropriately, and be careful about describing confidential departmental information, even in a network context. It is wise to use no more than one or two external examples in a portfolio, unless the role requires them, since assessors usually want to see how you perform in the grade's working environment. Where you do use one, link it to the role: say what you learned, and how it applies.

questions.prompt: Which activity can legitimately supply evidence for a senior application?

options.text: Occasionally helping to book a room for a network meeting
Reading the emails sent by a network you have joined
Chairing a staff network or leading a cross-government working group
Attending a social event organised by a staff group

questions.prompt: What makes external evidence work best?

options.text: Describing the activity in general terms so it applies widely
Showing scale, responsibility, decisions taken and results
Naming the organisation and the dates of your involvement
Mentioning the number of meetings attended in the year

questions.prompt: A candidate sits on a governing body. Which Behaviours might this evidence?

options.text: Delivering at Pace and Managing a Quality Service only
Developing Self and Others only, since governors mentor staff
None of them, because voluntary roles never count
Making Effective Decisions and Seeing the Big Picture

questions.prompt: Why should the candidate check the advert about unpaid experience?

options.text: Some adverts restrict whether it counts
Unpaid experience is always banned from applications
Unpaid experience is always included at every grade
The advert never mentions it, so the rule is the candidate's choice

questions.prompt: What care is needed about political activity?

options.text: It is always encouraged because it shows civic commitment
It is irrelevant to applications because it is outside work
It must be described in detail so that the panel can judge it
It may conflict with the requirements on civil servants, so check rules

questions.prompt: What is a sensible limit on the use of external examples?

options.text: As many as possible, to show a wide range of interests
None at all, since only work in the post can be counted
One or two in a portfolio unless the role requires more
One for each Behaviour, so that each has a fresh setting

questions.prompt: Why avoid claiming credit for others' work?

options.text: It overclaims and can be exposed at interview
It is acceptable if the group agreed the claim beforehand
It improves the statement by showing the scale of the work
It is expected, since network roles are always shared

questions.prompt: What else must be avoided when describing network roles?

options.text: Naming the network and its aims in the statement
Misusing official time or resources, or revealing confidential information
Giving a figure for the membership of the network
Mentioning that the network chair gave positive feedback

questions.prompt: Why do assessors usually want to see performance in the grade's own environment?

options.text: External examples are not usually true, so panels discount them
External examples are always weaker than work in the post
They need to judge how you work in the role's context
They want to keep the length of the interview short

questions.prompt: How should an external example be linked to the role?

options.text: Say what was learned and how it applies
Say nothing more once the activity has been described
Say that it was unpaid and done in the candidate's own time
Say that it was senior, without giving details of the work

items.title: L14: Confidentiality, security and fairness in your examples
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Examples drawn from senior work often involve sensitive material. Candidates must balance the need for specific evidence against their duties of confidentiality, security and fairness. Do not reveal protectively marked or commercially sensitive information in an application; describe the nature of the work in general terms and give the scale without exact figures if necessary. Phrases such as 'a significant programme of around a hundred million pounds' may be acceptable where the figure is public, but if in doubt, ask the department's security or the recruitment team. Do not include personal data about colleagues or customers: avoid names and use roles, and describe difficult conversations without identifying the person. This applies to performance cases, grievances and complaints in particular. The Civil Service Code requires honesty and integrity, so the description must be accurate and not distort to protect yourself or others. The Code also expects a civil servant to use official information only for its purpose, which includes not using confidential knowledge to gain an advantage over other candidates in a competition. Be wary of mentioning ministers, special advisers or political matters in a way that could breach impartiality or reveal confidential advice. When you are applying for a role in a different department, avoid assuming that terms of your current area are understood, and avoid inside information about the other department that you should not hold. If you were involved in a process that went wrong, describe your own role without assigning blame in a way that breaches confidentiality. If unsure whether something may be disclosed, leave it out or ask. Strong evidence can usually be given with generalised detail, as the assessor needs to see the judgement, not the secret.

questions.prompt: How should sensitive scale be described when exact figures cannot be given?

options.text: In general terms without disclosing protected figures
With exact figures, since the panel will treat them as confidential
By leaving out the example whenever sensitive scale is involved
By naming the project so that the panel can look up the figures

questions.prompt: Which is the right way to describe a difficult conversation with a colleague?

options.text: Name the colleague so that the panel can check the account
Describe their personal circumstances to explain the difficulty
Quote their words exactly to show the tone of the exchange
Use roles and avoid identifying the person

questions.prompt: What does the Civil Service Code say about information?

options.text: It may be used to prepare for applications if it is accurate
It may be shared freely within the department at any grade
It is always public once a minister has seen it
Official information should be used only for its proper purpose

questions.prompt: What is wrong with using confidential knowledge to gain an advantage in a competition?

options.text: It is unfair to other candidates and conflicts with the Code
It is allowed if the information is correct and relevant
It is not a problem for internal candidates in the department
It is wrong only if the candidate's manager objects

questions.prompt: Why take care with references to ministers and special advisers?

options.text: It is forbidden for any statement to name a minister
Ministers are irrelevant to evidence at senior grades
They could breach impartiality or reveal confidential advice
References to ministers make the statement too long

questions.prompt: What should a candidate do if unsure whether something can be disclosed?

options.text: Include it and note that it is sensitive in the statement
Leave it out or ask
Describe it in coded terms so that only insiders understand it
Assume that it is fine because it is not marked

questions.prompt: What does the assessor need from sensitive examples?

options.text: The full detail of the protected material to check accuracy
The names of the people involved in each decision
The classification marking of the underlying documents
To see the judgement, not the secret

questions.prompt: When applying to another department, what should be avoided?

options.text: Naming your current department in the example
Mentioning the grade at which you held the role
Assuming that terms from your current area are understood
Describing work that was done under a different line manager

questions.prompt: How should a failed process be described?

options.text: Naming those at fault so the panel can judge the account
Omitting your own role and describing the team's failings
Describing your own role without breaching confidentiality or assigning blame
Describing only the other team's mistakes and your response

questions.prompt: What is the Code requirement about description accuracy?

options.text: It may be softened where this protects a colleague
It may be exaggerated where the effect is positive for the service
It need not be accurate if the substance is clear

items.title: L14: Inclusion, fairness and values across the portfolio
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Success Profiles sit within the Civil Service values of integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality, and the Civil Service takes diversity and inclusion seriously. At senior grades, evidence of inclusive behaviour is expected within several Behaviours: Leadership (creating an environment where people can contribute), Working Together (including varied voices and ways of working), Developing Self and Others (fair access to development and opportunity), and Communicating and Influencing (accessible messages for different audiences). The question for a portfolio is whether the inclusion appears as a thread through the examples or as a single token paragraph. Strong inclusion evidence shows action with effect: you noticed that a group's views were missing and changed how a consultation worked; you adapted recruitment so that a wider pool applied; you changed meetings so that part-time or remote colleagues could take a full part; you challenged a decision that would have disadvantaged a group, and followed it through. Weak evidence offers a statement of belief or a list of training attended. Be careful with generalisations about groups, and describe individuals respectfully; never refer to someone's protected characteristics in a way that is unnecessary. Equally, the candidate should avoid presenting good intentions as results. Where the portfolio includes a recruitment or promotion decision, show that it was fair, evidence-based and documented. A related point is handling your own fairness at interview: if you know a panel member, or have a conflict of interest, declare it. The values also include honest self-presentation: examples should be true, and an inclusive story should not claim more than you did. If your role has given you limited chances to show inclusion, find a legitimate chance, such as leading a network, mentoring or reviewing a process for accessibility, before applying.

questions.prompt: Which values underpin the Civil Service Code?

options.text: Delivery, value, efficiency and speed in public services
Integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality
Loyalty to the minister, rank, tenure and obedience
Innovation, commercial awareness, risk-taking and growth

questions.prompt: Which statement describes strong inclusion evidence?

options.text: A statement of belief in inclusion and the candidate's commitment to it
Action with effect, such as changing a consultation after noticing a gap
A list of training courses on diversity attended in recent years
A mention of the department's policy and the candidate's compliance with it

questions.prompt: Why might inclusion appear as a thread rather than a single paragraph?

options.text: Single paragraphs are not accepted in a written statement
Threads use fewer words than a single dedicated paragraph
Paragraphs on inclusion are marked down by assessors
It shows inclusion is part of how the candidate works, not a token

questions.prompt: Which Behaviour would include creating an environment where people can contribute?

options.text: Delivering at Pace, which concerns planning and tracking of work
Managing a Quality Service, which concerns standards and customers
Leadership
Seeing the Big Picture, which concerns context and direction

questions.prompt: Which of these is weak inclusion evidence?

options.text: A list of training attended
Adapting meetings so part-time colleagues take a full part
Changing recruitment so a wider pool applied
Challenging a decision that would have disadvantaged a group

questions.prompt: What care is needed when describing individuals?

options.text: Always mention their characteristics so that the context is clear
Avoid describing the person at all, to protect their privacy
Use their names so that the example can be checked easily
Describe them respectfully and avoid needless reference to characteristics

questions.prompt: What should be done if you know a panel member or have a conflict of interest?

options.text: Declare it
Say nothing unless the panel member raises it first
Ask for a different job so that the conflict does not arise
Ask the panel member to leave the room without explanation

questions.prompt: How should a recruitment decision in the portfolio be described?

options.text: As quick and decisive, with little need for a written record
As personal to the candidate, based on their own judgement
As fair, evidence-based and documented
As confidential, with no mention of how it was made

questions.prompt: What should a candidate with limited opportunities for inclusion evidence do?

options.text: Describe a plausible example as if it had happened in the role
Claim others' work in this area as part of the team's output
Leave out inclusion, since it is optional in senior applications
Find a real opportunity, such as leading a network, before applying

questions.prompt: Why avoid presenting good intentions as results?

options.text: Intentions are never allowed in any written statement
Assessors score what changed, not what was meant
Results of inclusion work are always negative in practice
Good intentions are scored only in the interview stage

items.title: L14: Reading three candidate portfolios
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: A practical way to test your judgement is to compare sample portfolios. Imagine three HEO candidates applying for an SEO role that names Leadership and Making Effective Decisions as lead Behaviours, with Changing and Improving, Communicating and Influencing and Working Together possible at interview. Candidate A has one very large project, a transformation of an IT service, and uses it for every Behaviour, with the same savings figure appearing five times. The scope is high but the evidence is narrow and repeated, and the panel will wonder what else A has done. Candidate B has six examples of modest scope, well chosen to fit each Behaviour with clear results, but all are at the level of leading a small team. The portfolio is coherent and honest, but pitched below the grade for the lead Behaviours, and the candidate needs a larger example for Leadership. Candidate C has a mix: a cross-team change for Leadership, a difficult funding decision for Making Effective Decisions, a negotiation with a supplier for Communicating and Influencing, a short example from a staff network for Working Together, and a learning example about a delayed project. Scope rises to the target grade on the lead Behaviours, the examples are separate, and there is a balance of success and learning. C is the strongest, though C should check that the personal role in each example is clear. When you review your own portfolio, ask: where is my A, my B and my C? Most real portfolios have features of each. The remedy for an A is to widen, for a B is to raise scope, and for a C is to polish and rehearse. The best preparation is a candid review, with a mentor if possible, several weeks before the closing date.

questions.prompt: Candidate A uses one IT transformation for every Behaviour. What is the main weakness?

options.text: Too many examples for the number of Behaviours in the advert
Examples that are too small for the grade being sought
Narrow, repeated evidence from one project
Examples that are too old to be checked by the panel

questions.prompt: Candidate B has six small, well-matched examples. What is the main gap?

options.text: A lack of honesty about the candidate's own role in the work
Too much repetition of the same result across the answers
Examples pitched below the grade for the lead Behaviours
Too much variety in the kinds of work described

questions.prompt: Why is Candidate C's portfolio the strongest?

options.text: Scope reaches the target grade on lead Behaviours, with separate examples and some learning
It has the most words and the most figures of the three portfolios
It relies on the biggest project and shows the widest scope overall
It avoids any mention of setbacks, so shows the greatest confidence

questions.prompt: What does the same savings figure appearing five times suggest?

options.text: That the evidence is thin and the same facts are being reused
That the savings were large and deserve to be stressed
That the candidate is thorough and checks facts carefully
That the figure is reliable because it appears several times

questions.prompt: What does Candidate B need most for Leadership?

options.text: A shorter example covering the same project in less detail
A larger example
More adjectives to describe the leadership shown in each answer
A second small example from the same team to show a pattern

questions.prompt: What is the remedy for an A-type portfolio?

options.text: Add more figures to the single project used for every answer
Widen the range of examples
Shorten the main example so that it takes up less space
Remove the lead Behaviour from the application altogether

questions.prompt: What is the remedy for a C-type portfolio?

options.text: Polish and rehearse, and check the personal role is clear
Start again with a different set of examples before the closing date
Add more examples so that each Behaviour has two or three
Cut the learning example so the portfolio looks more confident

questions.prompt: Why include a learning example about a delayed project?

options.text: It lowers the scope of the application below the target grade
It balances successes with honest learning
It replaces one of the lead Behaviours with a weaker one
It is required in every senior application by the advert

questions.prompt: Which review method is recommended?

options.text: A quick check on the closing day after the statements are written
A review by the panel before the sift takes place
A review after the sift, using the feedback to improve interview
A candid review with a mentor, weeks before the closing date

questions.prompt: Why use a short example from a staff network for Working Together?

options.text: It can show collaboration across a wider group without a large project
It is the only valid evidence of Working Together at senior grade
It is always stronger than any example from the candidate's post
It is required by the advert for every senior vacancy

items.title: L14: Testing a portfolio with feedback and mock questions
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: A portfolio that has never been tested on another person is a draft. Several kinds of testing are useful, and each catches different faults. The first is a read-through by someone who does not know your work. Ask them to say, for each Behaviour, what you personally did and what changed; if they cannot, the evidence is too vague or too much about the team. The second is a read-through by someone who knows the work well, such as a colleague or former manager, who can tell you if a claim is overstated or an important contribution is missing. Their view is valuable, but remember that they may see the work through their own role. The third is a mock interview in which the questions are loosely worded, as real ones often are, and followed by probes such as 'What did you personally decide?' and 'What would you do differently?'. A mentor or someone who has sat on sift or interview panels can be especially useful, since they know what makes a score. Many departments run mentoring, coaching or sponsorship schemes for staff preparing for promotion, and it is worth asking whether one is available. Test your delivery too: record yourself answering and listen for long set-ups, vague verbs and missing results. Ask your testers for specific feedback, not general encouragement, and record what changes you make. Be aware that feedback can conflict; where two reviewers disagree, check against the advert's wording of the Behaviour at the stated level, rather than simply following the more senior person. Finally, allow time: feedback is only useful if you can act on it, so begin testing weeks, not days, before the deadline.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a read-through by someone who does not know your work?

options.text: To check that a reader can say what you personally did and what changed
To check the spelling and grammar of the statement only
To obtain a reference for the application

They are likely to be on the interview panel themselves
They may see the work through the lens of their own role

questions.prompt: What is the point of mock interview questions that are loosely worded?

options.text: Loose wording makes the questions easier for the candidate
Mock interviews should not resemble real ones

questions.prompt: Which follow-up probe is typical in a mock interview?

options.text: How many pages was your statement?
Who else applied for the post?
What did you personally decide, and what would you do differently?

questions.prompt: Why is a mentor who has sat on panels especially useful?

options.text: They know what separates higher and lower scores
They can change the scores given by the panel

They can predict the closing date

questions.prompt: What should a candidate listen for when recording a practice answer?

options.text: The accent and pace of the speaker
The number of seconds taken to breathe
Long set-ups, vague verbs and missing results
Whether the answer sounds friendly

questions.prompt: Two reviewers give conflicting advice. What is the sound way to decide?

options.text: Follow whichever reviewer is the more senior
Follow whichever reviewer was more positive
Include both versions in the application
Check against the advert's wording of the Behaviour at the stated level

questions.prompt: Why begin testing weeks rather than days before the deadline?

options.text: Panels read early applications first
Testing takes several weeks to arrange by law
The advert requires a record of testing
Feedback is only useful if there is time to act on it

questions.prompt: What should a candidate ask testers to provide?

options.text: Specific feedback on what they did and what could be sharper, not general encouragement
General encouragement to boost confidence
A prediction of the final score
A copy of the panel's marking guide
